Assuming East has 4 spades, he has only 6 known cards (4 spades and 2 diamonds). West has 7 known cards (1 spade and 6 diamonds). South can make the contract with the help of an entry squeeze. An entry squeeze is an ending that does not directly produce an extra trick, just an extra entry. The entry gained can be used, for example, to counter the threat of a one suit squeeze.

After cashing 1 round of spades, dummy's remaining spade honour should be played and overtaken with the ♠A. The ♣Q will now squeeze West instead of North. If West throws a heart, the spade loser that was just created is thrown from dummy. 4 heart tricks can now be taken by leading the ♥10 on the first round.

Discarding dummy's heart loser on the fourth diamond is unlikely to work as East will probably be able to ruff low. West will still have a trump trick. South should, therefore, ruff with the ♣10 and plan to squeeze East in the majors. East will have to have the ♥K, a card he has probably shown in the bidding and with his signal at trick 3.

A trick must be lost to the ♣Q. To retain a hand entry in clubs, which is necessary for the squeeze to function, South must duck either the first or the second round of clubs to West. Depending on which round of clubs is ducked and what suit West returns, a simple squeeze or a trump squeeze will develop against East.

Suppose West returns a trump after South ducks the first round of clubs. South can draw the last trump and cash another club pitching a heart from the dummy. East is trump squeezed. East must either bare his ♥K (South cashes the ♥A, ruffs the third spade, and scores the ♥Q) or come down to 3 spades (South ruffs out the spades and returns to the ♥A to cash the long spade).

If West had returned a heart after winning the ♣Q, South must win the ♥A. A trump squeeze is no longer possible. However, West's heart return has effectively performed a Vienna coup. East will be simple squeezed on the run of the clubs.

notes: West leads the ♠10 against 4♥. West's spade lead goes to East's ♠A. East's spade return goes to South's ♠J and is ruffed by West. West gets out with a trump. West's Unusual Notrump overcall and the early play have marked him with 1255 distribution.
The ♣A will take care of 1 of South's diamond losers. As East is known to have only 2 diamonds, his trump will make it impossible to ruff 3 diamonds in the dummy.

South's best chance is to play for an entry shifting trump squeeze. South must try to reach an ending like the above. When South leads the ♥Q, drawing East's last trump, West is squeezed. If West pitches a diamond, South's ♥Q holds. South can now establish a diamond trick by ruffing.
If, instead, West discards a club, North overtakes with the ♥K and a club trick can be set up by ruffing in the closed hand.

For such a squeeze to work, North and South must have an equal number of trumps at the time of the squeeze. The trump suit also must contain the ability to win the squeeze trick in either hand, depending on the defender's choice of discard.

South must win West's heart shift with the ♥A. There are several possible play sequences. South might as well concede a diamond right away. West wins the ♦A and returns a club (he needs to have both the ♣K and ♣Q for the squeeze to function).

The ♣A is won for a diamond discard and a club is ruffed by South. After cashing the ♠K, a diamond is ruffed low in the dummy. Dummy's last spade is ruffed by South. South has achieved a suitable matrix for the entry shifting squeeze. The ♥Q is played leaving West with no answer.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 6♥. South can easily succeed if West has 2-1 or 1-2 in the majors simply by winning the opening lead, drawing trump, and playing on spades. This line of play will not work if West is 1-1 in the majors.

If West was dealt 2 major suit singletons, East will have to gain the lead at some point in spades. East will return a diamond through South's ♦Q (West is very likely to have the ♦K) and North's ♦A will be knocked out. South will no longer have the timing to ruff both his club losers in the dummy while drawing trump and setting up and cashing a long spade.
The solution is an unusual example of keeping the dangerous opponent off lead. West cannot profitably attack the ♦A entry. South should duck the opening lead.

Assume West switches to a club. South wins the ♣A and ruffs a club. Next, he draws 2 rounds of trumps with the ♥K and ♥Q. Now, South takes the spade finesse and cashes the ♠A. After ruffing his last club in the dummy, South ruffs a spade. South can draw East's last trump and use the ♦A as an entry to the winning spade in the dummy.

A low club should be played from North. When East discards, his most likely shape is 7330 (West rates to be longer than East in both hearts and diamonds). If that is the case, the defense will be subject to a compound squeeze.
South should cash all of the clubs in the closed hand, overtaking the last round with North's ♣A. East must keep his spades and must, therefore, give up his guard in either hearts or diamonds.

If East discards a heart West will have the only heart guard. A double squeeze will operate with diamonds being the suit guarded by both East and West. South crosses in diamonds and cashes the ♠A. A heart is played to the dummy and the last club will squeeze both defenders, East in spades and diamonds and West in hearts and diamonds.
If East discards a diamond on the second last club a similar fate awaits the defense. Again there will be a double squeeze, but this time hearts will be the suit guarded by both defenders.

The last club is cashed immediately and South discards the ♦2. South crosses in diamonds. West will be squeezed in diamonds and hearts on the play of the ♠A. East will be squeezed in spades and hearts when the other top diamond is cashed.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. West's heart opening lead is taken by East with the ♥A. East returns a heart. South has 8 top tricks, 4 in spades, 1 in hearts, and 3 in diamonds. at first glance it appears South needs a favorable diamond lie or a successful guess in clubs to make the contract.

South can give himself a slight extra chance by ducking at trick 2. West continues hearts, East follows and South wins the ♥K. South should next cash 4 rounds of spades, followed by the ♦A. South then exits with his remaining heart. South should be careful to keep exactly 1 club in dummy.

If West began with 1 diamond, he will be forced to play a club and the defense will be powerless to prevent South from getting a ninth trick. If West is able to exit in diamonds, dummy wins. The contract will only be in danger if West began with exactly 4441 distribution.

If West's singleton club is the ♣A, South must exit with dummy's club before cashing the last diamond winner. West will win the ♣A and be endplayed into giving dummy the last 2 diamond tricks.This plan will also work if West's singleton club is the ♣Q. It will fail, however, if West's club is a smaller card.

South should instead cater to West holding a small singleton club (or the ♣Q) by cashing dummy's last diamond winner before leading dummy's club. If East follows small, South must put up the ♣K. South cannot afford to lose the lead to West (who has the ♦J to cash).

notes: West leads the ♣Q against 4♥. East wins trick 1 with the ♣A and switches to the ♠10. West covers with the ♠J and dummy wins the ♠K. South's 2 spade losers are not going away so South must avoid the loss of a trump trick.

While there are combinations that allow South to draw trump without losing a trick, South's chances are much better if he can engineer a 3 card ending where the defense is on lead and must give up their natural trump trick.

Since East did not respond to his partner's opening bid and has already shown up with the ♣A, East's only possible other high card is the ♥J. West must have the ♦Q and South should finesse in that suit immediately, first cashing the ♦K. After cashing dummy's ♦A for a spade pitch, dummy's last diamond is ruffed.

South cashes the ♣K, pitching a spade from dummy, and ruffs his last club in dummy. South exits a spade, endplaying West. West can do no better than to cash his other spade trick and lead the ♥Q, a card he is known to hold.
South should rise with the ♥K and finesse East for the ♥J. If West held that card he would have a balanced 15 point hand and probably would have opened the bidding with 1NT.

notes: West leads the ♠10 against 6♠. West's trump lead is won by South. South should cash the top hearts immediately and ruff a heart in dummy. The 3-3 break is good news but South is not out of the woods yet.
South could cash the ♦A for a club discard, ruff a diamond to the closed hand and play trumps from the top. The contract will make whenever trumps are 3-3.

However, West's lead of the ♠10 strongly suggests that East has a trump trick. If this is the case, South still has a chance by exiting with the fourth round of trump. If East has the ♣K and began with 1 or 2 diamonds he will be endplayed.

If South is willing to make the reasonable assumption that East has 4 trumps, there is a stronger line of play that does not depend on East's holding short diamonds. South should not cash dummy's ♦A. He should lead a small diamond instead and ruff in his hand. To prevent East from unblocking his spades and avoid being endplayed, South should be careful to ruff with the ♠4.

South cashes his top spades, revealing the expected 4-2 break. Despite East's efforts to unblock, South's ♠2 is just low enough to lose the lead to East. With East holding the ♣K, he is endplayed into giving South a way to dispose of his 2 club losers.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 7♦. West's spade opening lead is won in dummy. South's only possible loser is in clubs. If hearts are 3-3, there will be no problem. If hearts do not break the squeeze chances are excellent since West is certain to hold the ♠Q.

After drawing trump, South should cash the top hearts. If East has heart length, the contract is guaranteed on a double squeeze. On the last diamond West must abandon clubs to keep his ♠Q. Dummy discards the ♠J and East is squeezed in hearts and clubs.

When West has length in hearts, there are no entries for a simple major suit squeeze. If West has the ♣Q or ♣J, however, a guard squeeze will develop. On the last diamond West is forced to bare his ♣J. Dummy discards from either major.

South can now take 3 club tricks by dropping West's ♣J under the ♣A, and finessing against East's ♣Q. There is no ambiguity in the ending as West's last 2 cards are both known. If West had started with both the ♣Q and ♣J, the position would have been equally clear.

This form of guard squeeze matures with 1 loser. An opponent is squeezed in 3 suits. In 1 of the threat suits, the victim is protecting his partner against a finesse. There are no entries in either of the other threat suits, preventing a simple squeeze from maturing.

notes: West leads the ♥7 against 6♠. West's heart lead is taken by East. East continues hearts. South can afford to ruff high. When West follows it appears that South should have discarded a club at trick 2.
South's only possible losers are in clubs. Dummy has more than enough trumps to take care of South's 3 small clubs. South can, therefore, afford to draw 1 round of trump on which East discards.

South should continue with the ♣A and a club ruff in dummy. South should cross back to his hand by leading a heart and ruffing high. West's discard confirms the heart count. South leads another low club.

If West follows, South will either be able to establish the clubs or to cash the ♣K and cross ruff. When West ruffs in front of dummy, South must overruff with the ♠Q. West's remaining trump will prevent South from ruffing his last club loser. South is forced to draw trump and play for a squeeze.

South should run his spades without cashing the ♣K. On the last spade, East is subject to a guard squeeze. He must keep a heart winner and 2 clubs. East must therefore discard his diamond honor. South cashes his remaining high club (discarding dummy's heart) and finesses diamonds through West.

This form of guard squeeze matures with 1 loser. An opponent is squeezed in 3 suits. In one of the threat suits, the victim is protecting his partner against a finesse. There are no entries in either of the other threat suits, preventing a simple squeeze from maturing. For a guard squeeze to work against the defender to the right of the squeeze card, the threat in the hand with the squeeze card must contain a winner.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 6♣. West's wins trick 1 and continues with the ♠A for South to ruff. South's only loser is in hearts. He will need either a 3-3 diamond break or some kind of squeeze to succeed.

South should draw trump and probe the diamond distribution by cashing 2 of dummy's top diamonds. When West turns out to have diamonds stopped, a squeeze becomes necessary. If West has both heart honors he will be the victim of a simple squeeze between hearts and diamonds.
West cannot have both heart honors, however. West is a passed hand and has already shown up with the ♠A, ♠K, and a singleton club. With both heart honors as well he would have opened the bidding.

Fortunately, there is an alternative. If West was dealt 1 heart honor, a double guard squeeze will operate. South should run his trumps, taking care to discard the ♥J and to keep dummy's remaining spade.
On the last trump, West has no good answer. A diamond discard is immediately fatal. A discard of the ♥K will create a finessing position against East's ♥Q.
If West discards a spade East becomes the only defender with a spade stop. South discards dummy's small diamond. When South cashes dummy's last diamond winner, East is squeezed in the majors.

The double guard squeeze matures with 1 loser. A victim is squeezed in 3 suits. 1 of these suits is stopped by both defenders, but by discarding from that suit, the victim exposes his partner to a simple squeeze. In a second threat suit, the squeeze victim is protecting a finessing position against his partner. In the third threat suit the victim is the only defender with a stopper.
